title: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
hook: the sutras' boldest claim: love isn't the road, it's where the road goes
carry: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete
tomorrow: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete

segments.voice: Yesterday closed seva as vocation with the Gita's renouncer who never quits the job: do the work that's yours, without leaning on its fruit. Did you send something off and let it go? Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.
screen: `SEVA AS VOCATION.` · `NOT LEANING ON THE FRUIT.`

segments.voice: A road is usually a way to get somewhere. Nobody frames a photo of the on-ramp. You drive the highway to reach the beach, and once you're there, you forget the highway. Now, what if someone told you the road and the beach were the same thing? Year two opened a short book attributed to the sage Narada, the Narada Bhakti Sutras: its definition of bhakti as supreme love, and the four teachers' marks of it. For the next six days we read on, through to the last line. And a little past where we stopped, the book makes its boldest claim.
screen: `A ROAD, OR THE PLACE IT LEADS?` → `THE NARADA BHAKTI SUTRAS.` → `READ THROUGH TO THE END.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in paraphrase. Bhakti, the sutras say, is greater even than karma, jnana and yoga. Action, knowledge and the disciplined stilling of the mind, three great roads, and love is placed above them. That sounds like a ranking, and it is. But the next line gives the reason, and the reason changes how it sounds. Because it is of the form of the fruit. Phala-rupa. The fruit is what the tree is for. So the sutras aren't saying the other roads are worthless. They're saying love is what those roads are walking toward. Work done as an offering, knowing that clears the mind, a mind held still: in this book's view, they find their point in love. Then comes a second reason, and it's a surprising one. Because the Lord, the sutras say, dislikes pride and is fond of humility. The Sanskrit for that humility is dainya: lowliness, the state of someone with empty hands. A person can turn good work into a trophy. A person can turn knowledge into a trophy, and a long practice too. In the sutras' picture, love has a hard time doing that, because it keeps looking at the beloved, not at itself. That's Narada's view, and the text says so plainly. Other Hindu teachers weigh the roads differently. Shankara's school, which we met in year two, holds that knowledge is what frees, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Both are living Hindu paths. And the sutras themselves aren't done with the question. Tomorrow they ask, out loud, whether knowledge is the means to love, and they answer with a king and a meal.
screen: `GREATER THAN KARMA, JNANA AND YOGA.` · `PHALA-RUPA: LOVE IS THE FRUIT.` · `THE LORD LOVES HUMILITY.` · `NARADA'S VIEW, AMONG OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: empty hands. Sit comfortably, and let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up. Breathe. Notice anything you're holding up like a trophy today: something you did well, something you know, how long you've practiced. Don't scold it. Just set it down beside you, the way you'd put down a bag. Then rest with the hands open, nothing in them. If you pray, you can turn toward God with those open hands. If not, simply stay with what it's like to hold nothing up. The bell holds the time.
Bhakti. In the Narada Bhakti Sutras, not only a road but the fruit itself, and close to humility, dainya, the open hand.

Your line: bhakti: the Narada Bhakti Sutras complete. Today, when you catch yourself polishing a trophy in your head, set it down and look at someone you love instead. Day one thousand two hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: In devotional Hindu communities, the Narada Bhakti Sutras are studied in short sections with a teacher, and lines like these on love as the fruit and the Lord's fondness for humility are explained with stories of devotees.

match.prompt: love as the fruit — tap the pairs.
pairs: of the form of the fruit

myth: the sutras call karma, jnana and yoga worthless
they call bhakti greater, because it is the fruit those roads are walking toward.
the sutras say the Lord dislikes pride and is fond of humility
that is their second reason for placing love highest.
every Hindu school agrees that love stands above knowledge
that is Narada's view. Shankara's school holds that knowledge frees, with devotion readying the mind.

fork.setup: you've spent years on a discipline, and you're good at it. the sutras say love is greater. how do they explain that?
options: your discipline was a waste of time.
love is the fruit the roads are for, and the Lord loves humility.
love is easier, so it wins.
fork.reveal: the sutras give two reasons: bhakti is of the form of the fruit, and the Lord dislikes pride and is fond of humility. nothing is said to be wasted.

original.note: Sanskrit dainya, humility, lowliness: the sutras say the Lord is fond of it and dislikes pride.

trapdoor: what you thought: bhakti is the easy path for people who can't do the hard ones.
what it means: the sutras call love the fruit that action, knowledge and yoga are for.

what a scholar hears: sā tu karma-jñāna-yogebhyo 'py adhikatarā, phala-rūpatvāt: greater even than these, because it is the fruit; then a second reason, the Lord's dislike of pride and fondness for dainya.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind

notes: First day of the 'Narada Bhakti Sutras complete' block (1214–1219). Year two (days 693–694) covered sutras 1–6 and 15–24 (definition, the teachers' marks, the gopis); this block reads on from sutra 25 to the end, in six days.
Sutra numbering follows the common 84-sutra editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper prefers. Sutra numbers appear only in sources and the trapdoor, not in the voice.
